title: Premature Speech EOS is Not a Dominant Failure Mode in Qwen2.5-Omni: An Empirical Study of Text-Length-Coupled Audio Stopping

contributions.purpose: Test whether coupling speech stopping to generated text length improves speech-text consistency in an end-to-end omni-modal LLM.
contributions.mechanism: TLC-AS, a training-free decode-time intervention that computes a minimum audio token floor from text word count and a calibrated words-per-second rate, masking the speech EOS token until the floor is reached.
contributions.evaluation: Empirical study on Qwen2.5-Omni with VoiceBench CommonEval (200 samples) comparing WER with and without the intervention.
contributions.source_quote: We present an empirical study of TLC-AS, a training-free decode-time intervention for speech-text consistency, evaluated on Qwen2.5-Omni with VoiceBench CommonEval.

contributions.purpose: Establish whether premature EOS emission is actually a dominant failure mode in Qwen2.5-Omni.
contributions.mechanism: Measurement of early-stopping frequency under a raised audio token cap and of WER change under TLC-AS.
contributions.evaluation: Only 0.5% of samples show early stopping, and TLC-AS increases WER from 5.86% to 9.05%, i.e. degrades rather than improves performance.
contributions.source_quote: We find that premature EOS is not a dominant failure mode for Qwen2.5-Omni: only 0.5% of samples show early stopping, and TLC-AS degrades rather than improves performance.

contributions.purpose: Draw a methodological lesson about verifying failure modes before designing interventions.
contributions.mechanism: Attribution of the null/negative result to Qwen2.5-Omni's Thinker-Talker architecture already achieving good speech-text alignment.
contributions.evaluation: Supported by the 0.5% early-stopping rate and WER degradation (5.86% to 9.05%) under intervention.
contributions.source_quote: We provide insight that the Thinker-Talker architecture achieves good speech-text alignment without intervention, highlighting the importance of verifying failure mode existence before designing solutions.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Prior work on spoken language models has identified premature end-of-sequence (EOS) token emission as a potential failure mode in long-form speech generation (Park et al., 2024)... This motivates decode-time interventions that coordinate stopping behavior between text and speech streams.

We hypothesize that coupling the speech stopping decision to the generated text length—a mechanism we call Text-Length-Coupled Audio Stopping (TLC-AS)—could improve speech-text consistency by preventing premature speech termination.

notes: Explicit negative-result paper (declared in title and abstract): the target failure mode is rare (0.5%) and the proposed TLC-AS worsens WER from 5.86% to 9.05%. The paper's framing is that the hypothesized problem from prior work does not exist in this model.
